subtype: Approach: overnight resolution to change everything [Pitfall]
passage: Note, Sunday night. After Vaibhav's bad chemistry result on Friday, I watched him write a new timetable and pin it above the desk: lights out at nine at night, up at four in the morning, from the very next day. No half-measures. On Monday the alarm rang at four and he was up, grey-faced, and fell asleep on the sofa by five in the afternoon. On Tuesday the alarm rang and he did not get up. He dropped the timetable in the bin and said, "I can't even do this." What I did: I took it out of the bin, told him the plan was too big for anyone and not a sign of weakness, and asked if we could pick one small change together. He shrugged but sat down with me. We chose one thing: the same wake time every day. - Hansa

qa.q: What bedtime and wake time did Vaibhav pin above the desk?
qa.a: Vaibhav pinned lights out at nine at night and up at four in the morning.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when saying 'I can't even do this'?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt defeated and like a failure, after the plan collapsed in two days on top of a bad result.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav try instead of an overnight jump, and why?
qa.a: Vaibhav could fix one wake time and move bedtime earlier in small steps, because gradual changes are easier to keep than an unrealistic leap.

qa.q: How does Hansa see the failed timetable?
qa.a: Hansa sees a plan that was too big for anyone, and not a sign of weakness, which is why Hansa rescues it from the bin and offers a smaller start.

grounding: After a bad exam, the student resolves to sleep at 9 pm and wake at 4 am from tomorrow, and the unrealistic jump fails in two days and leaves the student feeling like a failure.

subtype: Approach: wind-down routine with if-then rules [Thinking]
passage: Lights-out at the hostel was eleven, but Tanvir had been awake until one for weeks. On Sunday he sat on his bed with a pen and wrote a rule the way his physics teacher wrote laws: if the clock shows ten, then the phone goes on the charging shelf in the corridor. He tapped the pen. A rule that said "try to" would melt at 10:05. Then the next part: after the phone leaves, wash face, brush teeth, read one chapter of a novel. Same order every night, so his head would learn that this sequence means sleep. Warden Uma Ma'am, who looked after the corridor shelf, nodded when he told her. "Every night?" "Every night." By Thursday the shelf held his phone at 9:58.

qa.q: Where does the phone go at ten under Tanvir's rule?
qa.a: The phone goes on the charging shelf in the corridor.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir avoid a rule that said 'try to'?
qa.a: Tanvir feared such a rule would melt away at 10:05, so he wanted a firm one that decides in advance.

qa.q: What could Tanvir do if reading stops working as a wind-down, and why?
qa.a: Tanvir could swap in a short, calm activity like stretching or writing tomorrow's list, because the repeated order of the routine matters more than the exact task.

qa.q: How does Uma Ma'am see Tanvir's plan?
qa.a: Uma Ma'am probably sees a responsible student who wants help keeping a rule, and is willing to look after the shelf.

grounding: The student decides that if it is 10 pm the phone charges outside the room, and a short routine of washing up and reading follows, giving the brain a repeated signal for sleep.

subtype: Approach: relying on caffeine and energy drinks [Pitfall]
passage: Dhruv, you asked why my results dipped in October, and I'll be honest: it was the chai and the cans. I'd finish my last cup of strong tea at nine at night and open an energy drink at ten, because I had chapters left and didn't want to lose the night. It worked for about two hours. My eyes were wide, my hands slightly jittery, and I felt clever. Then at one in the morning I lay there wired and tired at the same time. Next day I was so drained I needed two more teas before first period. The plan was making tomorrow's me pay for tonight's me. I'm Sunaina, and I've switched to water, and to stopping earlier.

qa.q: What did Sunaina drink at ten at night?
qa.a: Sunaina opened an energy drink at ten.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel at one in the morning, and what does it show?
qa.a: Sunaina felt wired and tired at the same time, which shows the drinks only masked the tiredness.

qa.q: What could Sunaina do instead to stay alert in the evening, and why?
qa.a: Sunaina could take a short break and finish the hardest topics earlier in the day, because rest helps focus more than strong drinks and does not delay sleep.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see the dip in Sunaina's results?
qa.a: Dhruv probably wondered what went wrong, and hearing the honest answer may help Dhruv avoid the same trap.

grounding: To stay alert, the student drinks strong tea and energy drinks late in the day, which masks tiredness briefly but delays sleep, so the next day starts even more drained.

subtype: Approach: tracking sleep and mood in a diary [Action]
passage: Okay, Ira, so my notebook. For two weeks I wrote bedtime, wake time, and a score out of ten for how focused I felt the next day. I expected no pattern at all. But look: on the four nights I got seven or eight hours, my focus was eight, nine, eight, nine. On the nights under six it was two, three, four. That isn't a lecture from Mum, it's my own handwriting. Something changed when I saw it. I stopped saying "I'm a night person" and started noticing that I couldn't follow chemistry after a short night. Now the notebook sits by my pillow, and the alarm goes off at the same time every day. I'm Eshaan, and I'm oddly proud of my little table.

qa.q: How long did Eshaan keep the notebook?
qa.a: Eshaan kept it for two weeks.

qa.q: What did seeing the numbers change in Eshaan's thinking, and how does Eshaan feel about it?
qa.a: Eshaan stopped saying 'I'm a night person' and started noticing the effect of short nights, and feels oddly proud of the table.

qa.q: What could Eshaan do next with the notebook, and why?
qa.a: Eshaan could try a week with a fixed bedtime and compare the scores, because a personal test shows what actually helps.

qa.q: How might Ira see the notebook data?
qa.a: Ira likely finds it convincing and interesting because it is Eshaan's own record and not general advice.

grounding: For two weeks the student notes bedtime, wake time and next-day focus, and sees focus is clearly best after seven to eight hours, a personal proof that motivates change.

passage: Wednesday. Day 6 of the morning plan. Wake at 6:30 no matter what. Curtains open first, the light hits my face and it actually helps. Then ten minutes of stretches, a short walk round the block with Siddharth from next door, and breakfast at the table: idli today. Last week I tried to force bedtime to nine and just stared at the ceiling. This time I'm not fighting the night; I'm fixing the morning and letting the night catch up. Yesterday I fell asleep at 11:20, about forty minutes earlier than usual, without trying. Siddharth says the walk is the best part. I think it's the breakfast. Tomorrow same again, 6:30, curtains, walk, idli or poha. - Madhav

qa.q: At what time does Madhav wake up in the morning plan?
qa.a: Madhav wakes at 6:30 no matter what.

qa.q: How does Madhav feel about the new approach compared with forcing bedtime?
qa.a: Madhav feels more relaxed and hopeful, no longer fighting the night, and pleased that sleep came earlier without trying.

qa.q: What else could Madhav add if sleep still comes late, and why?
qa.a: Madhav could keep the light-and-walk morning going for another week and dim the room earlier at night, because a strong morning anchor helps the body clock more than forcing bedtime.

qa.q: How might Siddharth see the morning walk?
qa.a: Siddharth likely enjoys it as company and says the walk is the best part, though Madhav thinks it is the breakfast.

grounding: The student sets a fixed wake time, opens curtains for daylight, does light exercise and has breakfast, since a strong morning routine helps the body clock more than forcing an early bedtime.

subtype: Approach: involving family in the routine [Action]
passage: In the hill town, the living-room TV stayed on until midnight for Papa's cricket replays and Ama's serials, and Gargi's room shared a wall with it. She had tried earplugs and a pillow over her head. On Sunday after dinner she sat between her parents and said, "I want to be asleep by eleven. Can the TV go off at ten and the house stay quiet? Just for a month?" Tenzin looked at Ama. "Even the replays?" "I'll watch them with you on Sunday afternoons," said Gargi. Ama laughed. "Agreed." On the first night the TV clicked off at ten, and the house went so quiet Gargi could hear the kettle cooling. By Friday even the dog had learned to settle early.

qa.q: What time did Gargi ask for the TV to go off?
qa.a: Gargi asked for the TV to go off at ten.

qa.q: How does Gargi feel when asking, and what shows it?
qa.a: Gargi feels a little nervous but determined, having tried earplugs and a pillow before deciding to ask, and offers a deal to make it easier.

qa.q: What else could Gargi do if the quiet lapses after a week, and why?
qa.a: Gargi could remind the family of the one-month trial and check in about how it is working, because a shared agreement is easier to keep when it is revisited kindly.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see the request?
qa.a: Tenzin is thoughtful and a bit reluctant about the replays but agrees, since Gargi offered to watch them together on Sundays.

grounding: The student asks parents to switch off the living-room TV at 10 pm and keep the home quiet, showing that changes are easier when the household environment supports them.

subtype: Approach: relapse after a festival or exam week and restarting [Revision]
passage:
Dear Shreya,

Thanks for not laughing when I told you about last week. My cousin's wedding meant four nights of bed at three and up at noon, and by Sunday my routine was gone. I sat there feeling as if I'd ruined a whole month of work. Then I remembered what you said: one slip is not a verdict. So on Monday I did only one thing: alarm at seven, curtains open, breakfast. No punishment, no marathon revision. On Tuesday I was tired. By Wednesday I was nearly back, and bedtime came on its own. I keep the wake time fixed and treat the rest as adjustable. Want to walk before school on Thursday?

Harsha

qa.q: How many nights did the wedding shift Harsha's sleep?
qa.a: The wedding meant four nights of bed at three and up at noon.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel on Sunday, and what changed?
qa.a: Harsha felt as if a month of work was ruined, but remembering that one slip is not a verdict made it possible to restart.

qa.q: What else could Harsha do to protect the routine before the next big event, and why?
qa.a: Harsha could keep the wake time as close as possible during the event and plan an easy morning the day after, because a quick restart is easier when the anchor is kept.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Shreya probably feels glad and useful, since the earlier advice helped Harsha to restart. 🙂

grounding: After a week of late nights around a wedding, the student does not give up but returns to the fixed wake time the next morning, treating the slip as normal rather than proof of failure.

subtype: Approach: seeking a doctor when routine change is not enough [Revision]
passage: For four months Irawati had done everything right: the same wake time, no phone after ten, a wind-down routine, no evening tea. Still she lay awake until three and woke exhausted, and the board exams were six weeks away. Her mother Aadhya had watched the dark circles and the swings between hope and despair. "It's not lack of effort," Aadhya said one Saturday. "Let's ask a doctor to look at this properly." Irawati hesitated. "Will they think I'm making it up?" "They'll listen." The doctor took a long history, asked about her days, and arranged a check-up and a follow-up visit. There was no quick answer, but for the first time Irawati felt that someone whose job this was had taken it seriously. She kept her routine while waiting.

qa.q: How long had Irawati kept the good habits?
qa.a: Irawati had kept the good habits for four months.

qa.q: What was Irawati worried about before seeing the doctor?
qa.a: Irawati worried that the doctor would think she was making it up.

qa.q: What could the family do if the exam pressure grows while waiting for the follow-up, and why?
qa.a: They could tell the school about the situation and keep the routine going, because support at school and steady habits make the wait easier.

qa.q: How does Aadhya see the situation?
qa.a: Aadhya sees a daughter who has tried hard with no result and decides that persistent sleep trouble needs a professional's assessment.

grounding: When months of good habits still leave the student sleepless and exhausted, the family consults a doctor, treating persistent sleep trouble as something professionals should assess.

passage:
Friday: The results went up on the board: 41 out of 100 in maths. Rehana walked home without seeing the road. She told nobody anything and went to her room and let herself cry. She made no plans that day.

Saturday: Her friend Rajni came over with a packet of biscuits and said nothing clever, only "That's rotten." Rehana talked for an hour. "I'm going to quit school and do the private exam," she said. Rajni looked at her. "Maybe not today."

Monday: Rehana wrote at the top of a page: "No big decisions until Thursday." Then she asked her teacher for the answer sheet. The disappointment had not gone, but the shock had.

qa.q: What mark did Rehana get in maths?
qa.a: Rehana got 41 out of 100.

qa.q: What does Rehana's note 'No big decisions until Thursday' suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: Rehana is still disappointed but steadier, and recognises that plans made in shock could be regretted.

qa.q: What could Rehana do on Thursday, and why?
qa.a: Rehana could look at the answer sheet and choose one small next step, because clear facts make a better base for decisions than shock does.

qa.q: How might Rajni see Rehana's idea of quitting school?
qa.a: Rajni likely feels worried and gently steers Rehana to wait, saying 'Maybe not today.'

grounding: After a low result the student allows a day of disappointment, talks to a friend and avoids big decisions, knowing that plans made in shock, such as quitting school, are often regretted.

subtype: Approach: analysing what happened with the answer sheet [Action]
passage:
Zeenat: got my physics paper back for the review today
Amandeep: and? how bad
Zeenat: 8 marks lost in section D, all unfinished. 3 in section B, careless units. 4 in C, I really didn't know that topic
Amandeep: so where's the biggest loss?
Zeenat: section D!! time. I spent 25 min on one B question 🤦
Amandeep: so not knowledge?
Zeenat: mostly not. I thought I was bad at physics. really I ran out of time
Amandeep: so what next?
Zeenat: timed papers, 10 min max per 4-mark question. and check units at the end 🙂

qa.q: How many marks did Zeenat lose in section D?
qa.a: Zeenat lost 8 marks in section D, all from unfinished questions.

qa.q: What does Zeenat now feel about physics after looking at the paper?
qa.a: Zeenat feels relieved and clearer: the problem was mostly running out of time and not being bad at physics, which feels more fixable.

qa.q: What could Zeenat add to the plan for the weakest topic, and why?
qa.a: Zeenat could revise the section C topic once, because the paper showed a genuine knowledge gap there worth four marks.

qa.q: How does Amandeep see the way Zeenat handled the result?
qa.a: Amandeep sees a clear thinker, asking questions that help Zeenat sort the losses and reach a next step.

grounding: The student requests the paper review, sorts lost marks into knowledge gaps, time management and carelessness, and finds poor time management in the last section caused most of the loss.
